Figure 1:Triangulating how “English (US)” becomes the default across the LLM pipeline.We trace this asymmetry across three connected stages:data exposure→\rightarrowrepresentation→\rightarrowgeneration,
using British English as the controlled reference, Ref(BrE). The study
jointly examines pretraining and post-training data, tokenizer behavior
and provenance, model prediction cost, and generated language. This
triangulation reveals where the American English (AmE) advantage first becomes visible, whether it persists across components, and how it manifests in model outputs. Its strength and form are examined across pipeline stages, developer countries (e.g., USA, UK, China, France, Italy, and UAE), prompt
conditions (e.g., default English vs. British English), domains and
sources (e.g., web, books, encyclopedic text, and mixed-domain corpora),
linguistic categories (e.g., orthographic vs. vocabulary contrasts),
registers (e.g., formal/encyclopedic vs. informal/conversational), and
alignment confidence levels. This breadth provides a deeper,
pipeline-level view ofstructural bias.

header: Appendix BDiAlign: Implementation, Validation, and Generalization

images.caption: Figure 6:Illustrative walkthrough ofDiAlign. Parallel AmE and Ref(BrE) passages contain matched contrasts in spelling, vocabulary, grammar, conventions, and multi-word usage.DiAligndecomposes each passage into overlapping 2–5-gram candidate spans, filters non-diagnostic spans, and compares the retained constructions against the American English (ID 17) and British English (ID 6) Google Books reference corpora. The resulting local evidence is aggregated into the regional alignment scores(PAmE,PRefBrE)(P_{\mathrm{AmE}},P_{\mathrm{Ref}_{\mathrm{BrE}}}).

images.caption: Figure 14:Timeline of independence across countries formerly under British colonization. The map highlights the wave of decolonization in the mid-twentieth century, when nations in Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, and the Pacific gained sovereignty. This geopolitical shift marked the decline of direct colonial governance but reinforced the institutional legacy ofBritish English (BrE)in education, government, journalism, and law across many of these regions(Tikly, 2016;Phillipson, 2018).
